title: The Curious Case of Benjamin Button at The Public #benjaminbuttonmusi...
transcript: Since crossing the pond to New York, Benjamin Button has already become one of the hottest tickets in town, and for good reason. It garnered a lot of hype in London for its folky score, poignant storytelling, and use of actor-musicians. Oh, and it doesn't hurt that it's already a widely beloved story. If you're new here, Benjamin Button follows a newborn old man as he ages in reverse toward infancy, trying to have a semblance of a normal life along the way. It's a good premise and the perfect soil for a generally sweet and borderline saccharine reflection on life, love, and time. It has its impactful moments, but I didn't leave thinking about the themes and lessons learned. It doesn't cut as deep as a show like Kimberly Akimbo, which is similarly sentimental, but much more bittersweet. Instead, I left this one in awe of the way it was executed. It's somewhat of a repackaged Once or Come From Away, with about a dozen actor-musicians assuming multiple roles each on top of underscoring their own story. The level of coordination that this production requires from an orchestration, music direction, and blocking perspective is pretty astonishing. The staging is so seamless, it's like you blink and suddenly everyone is in a new place on the stage. And on top of playing instruments, these actors make a hell of a vocal ensemble — the attention paid to the dynamics brings this already great score to the next level, giving it a cinematic quality that few musicals can achieve without flashy projections, for example. This production features the formidable Andrew Durand in the titular role, and while he gets to exemplify a lot of range portraying this character at different ages, I somehow felt like he was underused. Maybe it's just that I've seen him in more vocally demanding roles, or maybe it's the fact that despite being the central character, Benjamin isn't the most proactive protagonist. He has clear desires, but otherwise it seems like things happen to him as opposed to him doing things. Of course, he is restricted by his reverse-aging condition, at the whims of the universe and the sea, which is arguably the whole point of the story. We can't control how the wind blows, but we can cherish what each moment brings as it comes. I can't say that this changed my life, but I found it charming and certainly well-executed. I look forward to seeing it again when it inevitably transfers to a bigger stage.
reasoning: Creator praises the execution, staging, and ensemble highly but notes the story didn't cut deep and the protagonist felt underused. Ends with a clear recommendation and anticipation to see it again on transfer.
keyQuote: I found it charming and certainly well-executed.
